newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka wants private sector to build power plants.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka wants private sector to build power plants.

text.p: President Chandrika Kumaratunga on Sunday urged the private sector to build more power plants to meet energy needs which officials say will rise to 4,000 megawatts (MW) in Sri Lanka by 2015.

"I believe there is much interest in foreign and local private sector to participate in power generation in this country. I hope to enlist their support to fullfill the power needs of this country," Kumaratunga said.

Speaking at the inauguration of a new gas-fired power plant near capital Colombo built by the Ceylon Electricity Board, Kumaratunga said new power projects will mostly be built by foreign and local private joint ventures under build, operate and own (BOO) or build, operate and transfer (BOT) conditions.
The 115 MW Kelanitissa gas turbine power plant has been built by Italy's Fiat Avio at a cost of 2.1 billion rupees ($37.5 million).
It is Sri Lanka's largest power plant and capable of meeting one-fifth of the present national electricity demand or handle the peak load in the capital, Colombo, company officials said.
Demand for electricity is rising by 10 percent each year in Sri Lanka, and the by the year 2015 it will reach 4,000 MW, Jaliya Medagama, secretary at the Ministry of Irrigation and Power, said.
Sri Lanka which depends on hydro-electricity for 85 percent of power generation, can only increase the present hydropower generation capacity of 1,135 MW by another 500 MW, he said.
Last year after a drought crippled industry and hit the country, the government decided to look to other forms of power generation.
Before the Kelanitissa plant was commissioned, the country had 250 MW of thermal capacity, mostly diesel power generation plants.
Sri Lanka now plans to build a 300 MW coal-fired plant north of the capital Colombo to meet the rising demands.
"We will progressively reduce our dependence on hyrdopower generation to about 50 percent, while increasing thermal and other forms of power generation," Kumaratunga said.
She said her government had appointed two committees to formulate the country's power policy, one of which is studying the techanical aspects and ways to meet the rising demand.
